projects.title: 3D Physics Engine using C++ and OpenGL

projects.title: Face Mask Detection
projects.description: Designed a system used to face COVID-19. The system consists of 2 parts. First, a python software that is installed in closed buildings and uses computer vision to detect the number of people inside this place and whether they're not wearing a mask or adhering to safety precautions. Second, a map application that uses the data gathered from the python system to show the chances of getting infected at each place on the map.

projects.title: Electric purification

The prototype consisted of a container, 2 electrodes, wires, 2 9v batteries, and iridium magnets.

This past weekend, I had the absolute delight of trading sleep for grind at the Students@AI Hackathon in Seoul — and it was 100% worth it. Alongside my amazing team, Mara Dumitru and Shinnosuke Uesaka , we spent over 24 hours (no sleep unfortunately) building Hermex — a humanized AI tutor that transforms passive YouTube learning into interactive, engaging classroom-style sessions. Think of it as your favorite YouTube tutorial... but one that asks you questions back. Our goal? To make online learning feel less like a monologue and more like a dialogue. Our outcome? We were honored to win the Education & Civic Application (Tech for Good) prize! It was a blast with a team that ran on curiosity, caffeine, and barely any REM cycles. But more importantly, it was incredibly fulfilling to build something with the potential to improve how people around the world learn. Huge thanks to AI Consensus , Minerva University , and all the partners who made this event possible — and to all the other hackers and mentors we met along the way. It’s always inspiring to be surrounded by such passion and creativity. Grateful for the experience, the lessons, and the laughter in between the bugs. Here’s to more building, learning, and not sleeping (but maybe just a bit more sleep next time 😅). #Devlog 0 Hi Everyone 👋 I’m thrilled to share the journey of Catalyst, a personal project I’ve been working on. Catalyst is an AI-powered desktop assistant designed to simplify digital tasks like file management, Google Calendar events, Gmail, and more. Catalyst doesn’t just answer questions—it gets things done. A quick Intro; my name is Ahmed Ibrahim, and I’m a sophomore at Minerva University. I decided to work on this project because it will help me in my Uni journey and organize my workspace. It’s still a work in progress, but here’s a glimpse into the journey so far: ✅ React Frontend & Node.js Backend: * A React chat interface with Markdown and LaTeX-friendly responses * Designed a connection between the React, Node.js backend, and Python microservices. ✅ Implemented Manual Function Calling & Task Chaining: * Made the AI output a JSON response and gave it task execution codes that it can use and these codes are then parsed by the backend to call the functions required for each task. * Allowed Catalyst to execute multiple tasks in one response (Chained tasks) ✅ Integrated APIs for Core Functionalities: * Google Calendar: List and add events. * Gmail: Retrieve emails, send messages, and manage labels. * GitHub: Create and list repositories. * File Management: Create, edit, and append files. * News Retrieval: Fetch top headlines by query and category. * Google Contacts: List saved contacts seamlessly. ✅ Speech-to-Text & Text-to-Speech: * I’ve integrated Python microservices to allow for basic speech recognition and TTS. Looking for Your Input! I’d love to hear your thoughts: * What features would you like to see in an AI assistant? * Any suggestions for improving workflows or adding integrations? Feel free to check out my GitHub repo and contribute your ideas or code. activity.title: 🏘️ Let me live in your village for days! I’m making an intentional village where villagers know neighbors well, share things together, kids get to experience and learn from experience, and the whole village raises children together with love and warmth. Building many villages like this is the biggest dream of my life. And I am about to take my first journey to make it happen. Hi, I’m Youngeun – I introduce myself as Young n old “young” & “en”, a rising senior at Minerva University . I am obsessed with parenting and believe if the world is happy, everyone would like to become a parent. I believe true happiness comes from healthy love and community. Why am I so curious about parenting in my 20s? I view the world from the perspective of love and attachment. Babies need full attention and sensitive and immediate response from their parents. It is important to realize that family is a comfort zone and they will love you unconditionally. To do this, parents need to have a huge emotional capacity. Even if you know that you should not neglect the baby or respond discontinuously depending on your mood, if you don’t have that emotional bandwidth to digest your immediate emotion, you may react without thinking. When parenting is done in a close community, the burden of one parent can be lower. When you are busy, other neighbors could take care of the baby or play in a safe place with friends. Parents feel safe that there is someone looking after my child. However, nowadays, villages with a close community like this are few and far between . We’ve become accustomed to an apartment where we don’t know who is living next door. Friends and family live far away. This is why I want to bring back that humane, warm, close community through making villages so that stable love can flourish across the generations. 🌷To begin my journey of making villages, I plan to visit villages all around the world that have a close community and/or an alternative education curriculum. This trip is going to happen in September! If you know any of the villages that has their own culture to hold their community close and connected and/or has an alternative education system attached to it, please let me know. I would love to visit! If you know/visited/lived in/live in an intentional village, please let me know, I will truly appreciate it! If you found yourself interested in my point of view and want to talk more about it, please feel free to dm me. I’m more than happy to connect with you:D Feel free to share this post or tag someone who might be interested in this below!

activity.title: First milestone in my AI journey! I recently completed AI Connects, an intensive 10-day workshop hosted at German International University in Berlin (GIU Berlin) in collaboration with GIU and GUC Cairo- fully dedicated to the intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Medicine. Over the course of the program, we dove into: * AI applications in medicine & data exploration (PCA, clustering, KNN) * ML pipelines, feature extraction & PyRadiomics * CNNs, SVMs & evaluation metrics * U-Net architectures for medical image segmentation * Data augmentation, GANs & generative AI * Interpretability, uncertainty & federated learning As a capstone project, our team built MediSkin - an AI-Powered Medical Image Analysis Assistant designed to help people better understand minor injuries and skin conditions. What MediSkin does: - Detects & classifies visible injuries/skin lesions using a Vision Transformer (ViT) trained on the HAM10000 dataset - Generates patient-friendly explanations and first-aid guidance using an LLM (Llama 3.3 via Groq) - Sends medication & dressing reminders, with alerts to seek professional care when needed Built with React Native, Expo & TypeScript on the frontend, Express.js & FastAPI on the backend, and PyTorch powering the AI model - MediSkin is meant to support, not replace, professional medical care. Huge thanks to our supervisors Dr. Shadi Albarqouni , Dr. Nada sharaf, Dr. Rana A. Youness , and to my teammates for an incredible collaborative experience. Grateful to GIU and GUC for organizing such a hands-on, impactful program!

activity.title: Three summers ago, I came to Yale University for the first time. I had just finished my first year at Minerva University , and I had no idea that Yale Young Global Scholars would become a place I’d return to every summer. This year was especially meaningful because it was my first time serving as an Instructor. I taught nine seminar groups in Data Science topics, each with 13 students, co-led the Neuroscience & Psychology Capstone, joined the College Experience Panel to share with 250 students what studying at Minerva has been like, and watched lectures from Yale Professors and Researchers. But what I’ll remember most are watching students challenge each other’s ideas, ask thoughtful questions, and grow more confident over the course of the program. Preparing the seminars also made me realize how much Minerva has shaped the way I think about teaching. Over the past three years, I’ve studied across four countries, and every class has been built around active learning: discussion, collaboration, and learning by doing. Designing my own seminars gave me the chance to bring that same approach into the classroom, and seeing students genuinely engage with each other was easily the most rewarding part of the experience. A huge thank you to the incredible YYGS team, especially IST Program Manager Durel Crosby Sankofa , Track Coordinator Marvin Suarez-Pimienta, MS , my M27 classmates Galiya Askarova and Karolina Kędzia , who I had the pleasure of working alongside every day, and Breanna Patrice Ellison and Vitoria Souza Reyes who made our returners group complete ❤️ Now it’s time for one last year at Minerva. Next stops: Berlin 🇩🇪 and Tokyo 🇯🇵. I’m excited to see what this final chapter has in store.

activity.title: just got back from 2 days in sf for Y Combinator startup school. my brain is completely fried but the vibes were great. huge thanks to the yc team for putting this together (and free credits!) some takeaways: 1. do not take an overnight flight before an important event. idk why i convinced myself i could comfortably sleep on the floor at jfk for 6 hours, but i couldn't. i went into this running on zero sleep for two days straight. if i look dead in the photos, just focus on the background 2. listening to the top founders in ai. i really appreciate them giving up their time for free to talk to us. the most valuable part was getting to hear about some of the internal things happening at their companies, and hearing their advice on exactly what they would do if they were our age right now. it was also just reassuring to hear them debunk all the weird ai myths floating around the internet 3. sisp. had a breakout session with one of the partners about finding startup ideas and how yc evaluates them. they talked about avoiding "sisp" (solution in search of a problem). it sounds like common sense not to build tech just for the sake of it without a real problem to solve, but i didn't realize they had an actual acronym for it and screen for it that seriously 4. honestly, it was just nice to actually connect and hangout with people. not just "networking" to extract value from them, but genuinely just vibing with other builders
